content_voiceover: Acquired VWD syndrome, or AVWS, has three main mechanisms worth knowing for boards. Panel A is antibody-mediated, autoantibodies bind VWF and accelerate its clearance or directly inhibit its function, this is seen with lymphoproliferative disorders and autoimmune conditions like lupus. Panel B is the cardiovascular mechanism, and it's the one most likely to show up as a vignette, severe aortic stenosis, LVAD, or ECMO create high shear, turbulent blood flow that mechanically unfolds VWF, exposing it to ADAMTS13 cleavage, this selectively destroys the high molecular weight multimers and increases degradation fragments, functionally mimicking type 2A. This is the mechanism behind Heyde syndrome, aortic stenosis plus GI angiodysplasia bleeding, which resolves after valve replacement. Panel C is adsorption, malignant cells, particularly in lymphoproliferative and myeloproliferative disorders, adsorb VWF onto their surface and remove it from circulation. All three pathways converge on the same endpoint, VWF deficiency with loss of high molecular weight multimers and increased bleeding risk.
keypoints: AVWS mechanism A: autoantibodies increase VWF clearance/inhibition
AVWS mechanism B: shear stress (severe AS, LVAD, ECMO) degrades HMW multimers
AVWS mechanism C: adsorption of VWF onto malignant cell surfaces
High shear mechanism = Heyde syndrome (AS + GI bleeding), resolves post-valve replacement
keypoint_voiceover: Acquired VWD has three mechanisms, autoantibody-mediated clearance or inhibition, shear-induced degradation from severe aortic stenosis, LVAD, or ECMO which selectively strips high molecular weight multimers, and adsorption of VWF onto malignant cell surfaces. The shear stress mechanism underlies Heyde syndrome, aortic stenosis with GI angiodysplasia bleeding, which classically improves after valve replacement restores normal flow.
